Short answer: canceling a meeting is an explicit, communicative action that tells participants the meeting will not happen; deleting a meeting is typically a local/removal action that may or may not notify others. The two have different effects on attendees, resources, and records.

Key differences

- Who the action affects
  - Cancel (as the organizer): removes the event for everyone and usually sends a cancellation notice to all invited attendees and to any booked resources (rooms, equipment). Attendees’ calendars are updated to remove the event.
  - Delete (as an attendee): commonly removes only your copy of the event from your calendar. Other attendees keep their copies unless the organizer cancels. If the organizer deletes without issuing a cancellation, behavior depends on the calendar system (many provide a “cancel meeting” option to send notices).

- Notifications and communication
  - Cancel: generates outgoing notifications (cancellation emails/calendar updates) so participants know the meeting is cancelled.
  - Delete: often does not notify others (it’s a local change). Deleting as an organizer without using the cancel/notify option may or may not send cancellation notices depending on the client.

- Impact on resources and conferencing
  - Cancel: typically releases any reserved resources (room bookings, conference bridges) and may update the provider so the resource becomes available again.
  - Delete: if done locally by an attendee, resources stay reserved (until the organizer cancels or the resource booking is otherwise changed).

- Recurring series vs single occurrence
  - Cancel: you can cancel one occurrence or the entire series and notify attendees accordingly.
  - Delete: deleting one occurrence from your calendar removes your copy of that occurrence; deleting a whole series locally only affects you unless the organizer cancels the series for everyone.

- Organizer vs attendee permissions
  - Organizer cancel: authoritative—removes the event for all invitees.
  - Attendee delete: non-authoritative—only affects that attendee’s view, unless they have organizer-level permissions.

- Records, audit trail, and history
  - Cancel: leaves a clear record (cancellation notice, updated RSVP states) in email/calendar systems and often in audit logs in enterprise environments.
  - Delete: may leave no record for others; recovery and auditing depend on the client/server (some systems can recover deleted items).

- Best-practice implication (conceptual)
  - If the meeting is intended to be stopped for everyone, the organizer should cancel so everyone and the resources are notified. If an individual simply needs to remove it from their own schedule, deleting their copy or declining is the usual approach.

Variations by platform
- Exact behaviors vary by calendar client and server (Outlook, Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, enterprise systems). Some clients present “Delete” for organizers but will ask whether to notify invitees (i.e., perform a cancel). Others separate “Cancel meeting” (notify) from “Delete from calendar” (local).

Key differences (typical across calendaring systems)
- Who it affects
  - Cancel: affects all invited attendees (organizer cancels the event for everyone).
  - Delete: usually affects only the person who deletes the entry (an attendee deleting it removes it from their own calendar).
- Notifications
  - Cancel: sends a cancellation message/notification to attendees (so their calendars update and they are informed).
  - Delete: normally sends no notification to other attendees (unless the deleter is the organizer and the system treats their delete as a cancel).

- Calendar record and audit trail
  - Cancel: often leaves a record (event marked “canceled”), retains invitation history and may appear in archives or audit logs.
  - Delete: may remove the item from view and possibly go to a trash folder; audit/records depend on system retention policies.
- Resources and bookings
  - Cancel: usually releases resources (rooms/equipment) and updates resource schedules.
